description: METHOD.md §7.4: competitor level alignment of the one-time re-base to method 2.0 (PLAN-OF-PLANS §7.0). Generated once; the scorecard's v2 levels and met lists are the source of truth.
rule: A met check that relies on a third-party library counts at the framework's level only if the framework's own official docs recommend that library ('recommended'); otherwise ('other') the row scores the higher of: without that check at its level, or with it at the labs level (cap 39). 'not_met' checks are removed.

effect_ts.name: Effect-TS
effect_ts.notes: Official @effect/* packages wrap third-party drivers and SDKs (postgres.js, mysql2, tedious, better-sqlite3, @opentelemetry/*, Vitest); I counted those as `first` where the capability is reached through the official package API, and as `recommended` only where the user must install and configure the third-party library directly. Effect 4.0 (current as of Oct 2026) moved most former @effect/* modules into `effect/unstable/*` and made Prometheus export (observability/PrometheusMetrics) and property testing (effect/Arbitrary, with replay and model-based command arrays) first-party, so those checks are `first`; FSM checks other than #7 are `first` only through the v3 @effect/experimental Machine, which looks like a weak fit for fsm#1 (a transition table) and may be worth re-checking. Repo-process checks (sec.supply, test.qa#6, eco.*) concern the framework's own repo, so I treated them as `first`, not as a library dependency.

non_first.evidence: No FSM module in the effect v4 API index (https://effect.website/docs/v4/api lists Match, Metric and Mutable*, but no Machine or StateMachine). The v3 @effect/experimental Machine had no Mermaid/DOT export. Effect docs do not recommend XState.

Official v3 integration packages in Effect-TS/effect document using these query builders. @effect/sql has no query builder of its own. Neither integration package is in the v4 package list at https://effect.website/docs/v4/api.
https://effect.website/docs/v4/observability/tracing sets up NodeSdk from @effect/opentelemetry with @opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base. Sampling comes from the OTel SDK, not from Effect's own OtlpTracer.
The official @effect/vitest package (in the v4 API package list) wraps Vitest, and its docs make Vitest the test runner. Snapshot support is Vitest's.
Shuffling tests with a reproducible seed is a Vitest runner option, reached through the official @effect/vitest integration. Effect itself has no such feature.

otp.name: OTP
otp.notes: rebar3, Hex, cowboy and RabbitMQ appear on erlang.org/community only as a 'Popular Erlang Applications' list, so I treated them as popularity rather than a doc recommendation (other); count them as recommended instead if the owner accepts that page. The only clear official-doc recommendation found is the property-testing tools (PropEr/EQC/Triq) named in the ct_property_test reference docs. Process checks (sec.supply, eco.*) and borderline judgements (web.rpc#1/#6 met via ASN.1 extensibility, dx.diagnostics#6 via OTP's bundled Emacs mode, sec.config#2 env layer via ERL_FLAGS) were left as first.

non_first.evidence: OTP ships no cache API that can swap in a Redis or Memcached backend, and no Redis or Memcached client. ets and mnesia are first-party but are not Redis/Memcached. Close to not_met because no Erlang library is known to put local and Redis caching behind one API.

inets httpd terminates TLS but only speaks HTTP/1.1, so HTTP/2 needs cowboy. Cowboy appears only under 'Popular Erlang Applications' on https://www.erlang.org/community, a popularity list rather than a doc recommendation.
OTP has no single contract that runs over several transports (HTTP plus WebSocket/binary). ASN.1 and erpc each cover only one part.
OTP logger does not link log records to traces or spans. The OTel Erlang SDK is maintained by CNCF and is not mentioned in the OTP docs.
OTP has erlang:statistics and system_info but no global metric registry you can snapshot. The OTP docs do not recommend a metrics library.
OTP has seq_trace and the dbg/trace BIFs, but no span API with attributes.
OTP has no OTLP export.
OTP does not propagate W3C trace-context or baggage.
inets httpd does not create spans automatically.
Sampling settings and OTEL_* environment variables come only from the OTel SDK.
The logging facade is first-party (logger), but OpenTelemetry interop needs the third-party OTel SDK, which the OTP docs do not mention.
OTP has no Kafka client.
OTP has no AMQP client. RabbitMQ appears only in the community page's popular-apps list.
Broker ack/nack and dead-lettering come from the client library and the broker.
OTP has no broker consumer abstraction.
OTP has no SMTP client and no email-provider API clients.
OTP has no MIME mail composer.

https://www.erlang.org/doc/apps/common_test/ct_property_test.html says one of Erlang QuickCheck, PropEr or Triq 'is assumed to be installed'. ct_property_test is OTP's documented way to do property testing.
PropEr builds generators from -type/-spec declarations. It is documented through ct_property_test.
Shrinking is done by the property tool that ct_property_test relies on.
The Common Test User's Guide property-testing chapter (ct_property_test statem helpers) uses these tools.
Failing cases are kept and replayed with proper:counterexample/proper:check. Persistence across runs is weak.

OTP has no project generator. rebar3 is listed only under 'Popular Erlang Applications' on erlang.org/community. The OTP system docs mention rebar3 only for ex_doc (system/documentation.html), not for scaffolding.
Same source as dx.scaffold#1.
OTP has no dev run command with dev defaults. The plain erl shell needs manual -pa and -config flags.
OTP has no dev/test/prod profile mechanism, only sys.config files picked by hand.
Dialyzer, xref and compiler warnings are not documented with bad/good examples per rule. Elvis rules are. The OTP docs do not mention Elvis.

rails.name: Rails
rails.notes: I classed default-Gemfile gems as first, following the 'Rails 8 defaults are first' rule. That covers Puma, Thruster, bootsnap, Brakeman, rubocop-rails-omakase, capybara/selenium, bcrypt (added by the auth generator) and Thor (rails/thor); concurrent-ruby and connection_pool are only transitive dependencies of Rails components. Only two gems are actually recommended in the official guides: rack-cors (security guide) and rails-i18n (i18n guide). The other de facto gems (Devise, Pundit, graphql-ruby, OpenTelemetry, ActiveAdmin, AASM, RES, Karafka, RubyLLM) are at most mentioned in passing or absent, so they fall to other. I judged the checks resting on Rails 8.1 features as first: ActiveJob::Continuable for fault.workflows#1-2, Rails.event, and Mission Control Jobs as a rails-org package; confirm the snapshot credited those rather than third-party gems such as acidic_job or sidekiq-web.

django.name: Django
django.notes: Django's docs almost never name third-party packages directly. Instead topics/tasks, topics/email and ref/files/storage link to the official Community Ecosystem page (djangoproject.com/community/ecosystem). I counted packages as recommended only when a docs page links that page for the same concern (django-storages, django-anymail, django-tasks-db/huey); packages that are on the page but not linked from the relevant docs page (django-allauth, django-environ, factory_boy) count as other. Packages owned by the DSF but outside the stated scope (Channels, Daphne, asgiref, django-asv) are judged by the docs rule, which makes Channels other; Python stdlib/asyncio items, DRF features and Django 6.0 built-ins (CSP middleware with nonces, the django.tasks API) are first and so not listed.

laravel.name: Laravel
laravel.notes: Most 'met' checks that are not first-party fall into third-party areas with no Laravel doc endorsement: OpenTelemetry, GraphQL (Lighthouse), event sourcing, OpenAPI, Larastan, Spatie packages. Only Livewire, Inertia, Vite, Mockery and PHPUnit/Pest qualify as 'recommended', because laravel.com docs document them explicitly. Several things count as first-party despite being commercial or bundled dependencies: Nova, Forge, Vapor, Cloud, Nightwatch, the Laravel AI SDK (laravel/ai, documented at laravel.com/docs/ai-sdk) and laravel/mcp, plus Guzzle, Monolog, Flysystem and Symfony Console bundled behind first-party facades. Two timeout checks (core.ergonomics#4, core.race#1) look over-credited in the snapshot, so they are marked not_met.

non_first.evidence: Laravel has no generic one-call timeout for an arbitrary closure. Timeouts exist only per subsystem: Http::timeout, Process::timeout, and the job $timeout property (https://laravel.com/docs/12.x/queues#timeout).
Laravel has no timeout combinator that returns an optional result. PHP is synchronous and Laravel adds no general-purpose timeout. Same reason as core.ergonomics#4.
Laravel has no first-party state machine, and the official docs do not document a state-machine package.
Declarative state definitions come only from community packages. The official docs do not mention any.
Transition actions and entry/exit hooks come only from community packages.
Validation rules and API Resources are separate first-party constructs. One definition that both decodes and encodes needs spatie/laravel-data, which the official docs do not mention.
Generating the schema from a typed class is not first-party. Laravel FormRequest rules are hand-written arrays.
No first-party OpenAPI generator, and none is referenced in the laravel.com docs.
The Swagger/Stoplight docs UI is served by Scramble or l5-swagger, not by Laravel.

Mapping constraints into the spec is done by Scramble's rule inference.

nextjs.name: Next.js
nextjs.notes: Core runtime checks (async/await, AbortSignal.timeout, Promise.any, Web Streams, worker_threads, Intl) are counted as first because they come from the language/runtime, and Vercel Workflow, Queues, Cron, @vercel/otel, the AI SDK (including MCP) and eslint-config-next are counted as first under the Vercel-maintained rule. The weakest calls are obs.metrics (recommended only because the docs' OpenTelemetry guide shows the manual OTel SDK; it is not a metrics-specific recommendation) and data.cache#2 (first-party handler interface, Redis client never named). Data access is the big gap: nextjs.org/docs only says 'an ORM or database' and never names Prisma, Drizzle or any SQL client, so the whole data.sql/orm/migrations/backends block is other.
